Tselem
TSEH-lem
n. (Hebrew)
Hebrew tselem, “image, likeness, representation,” from a root meaning to carve or to shadow. The Greek LXX renders it eikōn, image; the NT picks up the language for Christ as the eikōn of the invisible God.

📖 Biblical Definition

Tselem is the Hebrew word for image or likeness, and its supreme biblical occurrence is at the creation of man in Genesis 1:26-27: and God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness... So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. The doctrine that flows from this single text is one of the deepest in biblical anthropology. Every human being is created in the image of God (tselem ’Elohim): male and female, child and adult, born and unborn, intelligent and developmentally disabled, healthy and dying, of every ethnicity and tribe—each bears the image of the Creator and is to be treated accordingly. The image-doctrine grounds the biblical sanctity of human life (Gen 9:6: whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man—capital punishment for murder grounded explicitly in the image), the biblical equality of all human persons (every person bears the image, regardless of natural distinctions), and the biblical dignity of every neighbor (James 3:9 grounds the warning against cursing one’s fellow-man in the fact that therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God). The fall has marred the image but has not erased it: Adam after the fall begets Seth in his own likeness, after his image (Gen 5:3)—the image persists in fallen humanity, though damaged. Christ is the perfect image: Colossians 1:15, who is the image (eikōn) of the invisible God; 2 Corinthians 4:4, the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God; Hebrews 1:3, the express image of his person. The redemptive trajectory of the doctrine is the restoration and consummation of the image in the redeemed. The saints are being renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him (Col 3:10); they are predestinated to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29); and at the consummation, we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The image-doctrine therefore traces a structural arc across the canon: created in the image, marred by the fall, restored in Christ the perfect image, progressively renewed in His people through sanctification, consummated at the resurrection when the saints shall fully bear the image of the heavenly. Apart from the image-doctrine, biblical anthropology collapses; with it, the dignity of every human person, the equality of all bearers of the image, and the trajectory of the redeemed toward conformity to Christ all stand.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Hebrew term.) Tselem: image, likeness, representation; the Hebrew word at the creation of man (Gen 1:26-27, in the image of God); the foundational anthropological doctrine grounding the dignity of every human person and the redemptive trajectory toward conformity to Christ, the perfect image (Col 1:15).

IMAGE, n. — A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance, as wood, stone, brass, or marble. In scripture, the resemblance of God impressed upon the soul of man at his creation; that conformity to the divine character which is the proper end of redemption.

TSELEM — (Hebrew noun, H6754.) Image, likeness, representation. The keyword of Gen 1:26-27 (man created in the image of God); subsequently grounding the sanctity of human life (Gen 9:6), the equality of all bearers of the image, and the redemptive trajectory toward conformity to Christ, the perfect eikōn (Col 1:15).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 1:26-27 — "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness... So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

Genesis 9:6 — "Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."

Colossians 1:15 — "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature."

Romans 8:29 — "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The image-of-God doctrine is corrupted, in the contemporary moral landscape, by the systematic denial of the image in classes of human beings (the unborn killed in abortion, the disabled discarded as inconvenient, the elderly euthanized as no-longer-productive)—and by the ideological inflation of the image into a basis for autonomous self-definition that severs the image from its Creator and treats the bearer as the author of his own being.

expand to see more

The systematic denial of the image in classes of human beings is the most pressing contemporary corruption. The unborn child in the womb is, by biblical doctrine, an image-bearer from conception, and the deliberate killing of image-bearers (which abortion is) is the unjust shedding of innocent blood. The developmentally disabled person who cannot speak for himself is, by biblical doctrine, an image-bearer of equal dignity to the philosopher and the surgeon; the discarding of such persons as inconvenient or unproductive is the denial of the image. The elderly person whose productive capacities have declined is, by biblical doctrine, an image-bearer whose dignity is not measured by his output; the euthanizing of the elderly is the active denial of the image. The recovery of the image-doctrine is therefore one of the most pressing pastoral and political tasks of the present age: the unqualified affirmation that every human being, at every stage of life and in every condition, bears the image of God and is to be treated accordingly. The biblical sanctity of human life flows from this image-doctrine; remove the image, and the sanctity collapses; restore the image, and the sanctity is restored along with it.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the ideological inflation of the image into a basis for autonomous self-definition that severs the image from its Creator. Made in the image of God is read as: I have the inherent right to define myself however I choose, with my self-definition having the same dignity as God’s creation of me. The biblical doctrine refuses this. The image is given by the Creator; it is His image (not mine); it has a definite form (male and female, created and creaturely, designed and not self-authored); and the redemptive trajectory of the image is conformity to Christ, the perfect Image, not self-construction along whatever lines the bearer prefers. The contemporary identity-politics use of the image-language (the affirmation that every form of self-identification must be respected because each person is made in the image) is a corruption of the doctrine that has retained the vocabulary while reversing the substance. Recover both ends. Refuse the denial of the image in classes of human beings, and refuse the ideological inflation that severs the image from its Creator. The biblical image-doctrine is the foundation of human dignity precisely because it locates that dignity not in the bearer’s self-construction but in the Creator’s gift—a gift that grounds the sanctity of every human life and the trajectory of every redeemed soul toward conformity to the perfect Image Jesus Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tselem (image, likeness, representation), at Gen 1:26-27 the keyword of biblical anthropology; Greek eikōn the NT equivalent; tracing the structural arc from creation in the image, through the fall’s marring, to Christ the perfect image (Col 1:15) and the saints’ redemptive conformity to Him (Rom 8:29).

expand to see more

Hebrew tselem (H6754) — image, likeness, representation (Gen 1:26-27; 5:3; 9:6; Ps 39:6; 73:20).

Hebrew d’mūth (H1823) — likeness, similitude (paired with tselem at Gen 1:26).

Greek eikōn (G1504) — image (Col 1:15; 3:10; 2 Cor 3:18; 4:4; Rom 8:29; 1 Cor 11:7; 15:49; Heb 1:3 cognate charaktēr).

Greek homoiōsis (G3669) — likeness, resemblance (Jas 3:9, the “similitude of God”).

Usage

"In the image of God created he him; male and female created he them—the foundational anthropological doctrine of every human bearing the image of God."

"Christ is the perfect eikōn (Col 1:15), and the saints are being conformed to His image (Rom 8:29)—the image’s redemptive trajectory."

"Denial of the image in classes of human beings (unborn, disabled, elderly) and ideological inflation severing the image from its Creator are opposite contemporary corruptions; biblical doctrine grounds dignity in the Creator’s gift, not in self-construction."
